items.stem: Explain why nitrogen is used to fill food packaging.
items.answer: It is very unreactive (strong triple bond, non-polar) so it does not oxidise food or support microbial growth.

items.stem: Explain why ammonia is described as a weak base.
items.answer: It only partially reacts with water to form NH₄⁺ and OH⁻; the equilibrium lies to the left.
items.markingKey: partial reaction [1]; equilibrium to left [1]

items.answer: (a) NH₃ pyramidal 107° (one lone pair); NH₄⁺ tetrahedral 109.5° (no lone pair). (b) Lone pair on N accepts a proton.

items.stem: What is the shape of the ammonium ion?
items.answer: tetrahedral

items.stem: Explain why farmers should not add calcium hydroxide to soil at the same time as ammonium fertilisers.
items.answer: Calcium hydroxide (a base) reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost.
items.markingKey: base reacts with NH₄⁺ [1]; NH₃ lost [1]

items.stem: Explain why the bond angle in NH₄⁺ (109.5°) is larger than in NH₃ (107°).
items.answer: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair has become a bonding pair (dative bond to H⁺), so all four pairs repel equally.
items.markingKey: lone pair used in bonding [1]; four bonding pairs repel equally [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Ana states: "Nitrogen is unreactive because it is a noble gas." Explain why this statement is incorrect.

items.stem: Explain how a catalytic converter reduces pollution from nitrogen oxides.
items.answer: NO is reduced to N₂ by reaction with CO (oxidised to CO₂) on the surface of a Pt/Rh catalyst: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.
items.markingKey: NO reduced to N₂, CO oxidised [1]; equation/catalyst [1]

items.stem: A car exhaust contains 2.0 g of nitrogen monoxide per kilometre. In the catalytic converter it reacts: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. Calculate the mass of carbon monoxide needed to remove all of the NO and the volume of nitrogen formed at r.t.p. per kilometre. State which species is oxidised.
items.answer: 1.87 g CO; 0.800 dm³ N₂; CO is oxidised (C +2 → +4)
items.markingKey: n(NO) = 2.0/30.0 = 0.0667 mol [1]; CO 1 : 1 so 1.87 g [1]; n(N₂) = 0.0333 mol, V = 0.800 dm³ [1]; CO oxidised, NO reduced [1]

items.stem: Air monitoring in Auckland on a sunny day shows NO peaking at about 08:00, NO₂ peaking at about 10:00 and ozone peaking at about 14:00. Explain the order of these peaks.
items.answer: NO is emitted by morning rush-hour traffic; it is oxidised to NO₂ over the next hours (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂); NO₂ is photolysed in strong afternoon sunlight (NO₂ → NO + O, O + O₂ → O₃) and reacts with hydrocarbons, so ozone/PAN peak in early afternoon.
items.markingKey: NO from traffic [1]; oxidation to NO₂ [1]; sunlight needed for ozone/PAN formation [1]

items.stem: Air monitoring in Seoul on a sunny day shows NO peaking at about 08:00, NO₂ peaking at about 10:00 and ozone peaking at about 14:00. Explain the order of these peaks.
items.answer: NO is emitted by morning rush-hour traffic; it is oxidised to NO₂ over the next hours (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂); NO₂ is photolysed in strong afternoon sunlight (NO₂ → NO + O, O + O₂ → O₃) and reacts with hydrocarbons, so ozone/PAN peak in early afternoon.
items.markingKey: NO from traffic [1]; oxidation to NO₂ [1]; sunlight needed for ozone/PAN formation [1]

items.stem: Sofia is writing a report on how nitrogen oxides from vehicles affect air quality. (a) Describe how photochemical smog forms. (b) State one health effect of photochemical smog.
items.answer: (a) NO₂ and unburnt hydrocarbons react in sunlight to form ozone and PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate). (b) Respiratory irritation, eye irritation, asthma.
items.markingKey: (a) NO₂ and unburnt hydrocarbons react in sunlight to form ozone and PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate). [2] (b) Respiratory irritation, eye irritation, asthma. [1]

items.stem: Felix is writing a report on how nitrogen oxides from vehicles affect air quality. (a) Write an equation for the oxidation of NO in air. (b) Write an equation for the removal of NO in a catalytic converter and identify the oxidising agent. (c) Explain the role of NO₂ in the formation of acid rain.
items.answer: (a) 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (b) 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂; NO is the oxidising agent. (c) It catalyses oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃; it also forms nitric acid.
items.markingKey: (a) 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ [1] (b) 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂; NO is the oxidising agent. [2] (c) It catalyses oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃; it also forms nitric acid. [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which acid is formed when SO₃ dissolves in rainwater? (b) What type of catalyst is NO₂ in the atmospheric oxidation of SO₂?
items.answer: (a) sulfuric acid (b) homogeneous
items.markingKey: (a) SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄. (b) Gas-phase catalyst with gaseous reactants.

items.stem: Zara writes in a revision note: "NO₂ is used up when it speeds up the oxidation of SO₂." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. NO₂ is regenerated (NO + ½O₂ → NO₂), so it acts as a catalyst.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Arjun writes in a revision note: "Acid rain is caused mainly by carbon dioxide." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. CO₂ makes rain only slightly acidic (pH ~5.6); acid rain is caused by SO₂ and NOx.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Amara is studying acid rain caused by emissions from a diesel-powered ship near Toronto. Write an equation for the formation of sulfuric acid in rainwater; describe one effect of acid rain on buildings or lakes, with an equation where possible.
items.answer: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; limestone/marble is eroded: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O; lakes become acidic, harming fish
items.markingKey: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ [1]; effect described [1]; CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O [1]

items.stem: Rain falling near an industrial city in Madrid has a pH of 4.2. (a) Write equations for the formation of SO₂ from burning sulfur impurities and its oxidation to SO₃ catalysed by NO₂. (b) Explain why rain is slightly acidic even in unpolluted air.
items.answer: (a) S + O₂ → SO₂; SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂ (b) Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid (pH about 5.6).
items.markingKey: (a) S + O₂ → SO₂; SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂ [3] (b) Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid (pH about 5.6). [1]

items.stem: Which gas is produced when ammonium chloride is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
items.answer: ammonia
items.markingKey: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O; turns damp red litmus blue.

items.stem: A fertiliser company in Kathmandu sells ammonium salts. Explain why the bond angle in NH₄⁺ (109.5°) is larger than in NH₃ (107°).
items.answer: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair has become a bonding pair (dative bond to H⁺), so all four pairs repel equally.
items.markingKey: lone pair used in bonding; four bonding pairs repel equally [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the bond angle in NH₄⁺ (109.5°) is larger than in NH₃ (107°). (b) Explain why ammonia is described as a weak base.
items.answer: (a) In NH₄⁺ the lone pair has become a bonding pair (dative bond to H⁺), so all four pairs repel equally. (b) It only partially reacts with water to form NH₄⁺ and OH⁻; the equilibrium lies to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) lone pair used in bonding [1]; four bonding pairs repel equally [1] (b) partial reaction [1]; equilibrium to left [1]

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in the fertiliser ammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₃PO₄.
1.070 g of ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl, is warmed with excess sodium hydroxide. Write an ionic equation and calculate the volume of ammonia released at r.t.p., in cm³.
items.answer: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O; 480 cm³
items.markingKey: ionic equation [1]; n(salt) = 1.070/53.5 = 0.0200 mol, n(NH₃) = 0.0200 mol [1]; V = 480 cm³ [1]

items.stem: A farmer in Seoul uses ammonium chloride as a fertiliser. (a) Explain why nitrogen gas is unreactive. (b) Explain why ammonia is a Brønsted–Lowry base.
items.answer: (a) Strong N≡N triple bond (944 kJ mol⁻¹); non-polar. (b) Lone pair on N accepts a proton.
items.markingKey: (a) Strong N≡N triple bond (944 kJ mol⁻¹); non-polar. [2] (b) Lone pair on N accepts a proton. [1]

items.stem: Mei heats ammonium sulfate with calcium hydroxide in a school laboratory to make ammonia. (a) Explain why ammonia is a Brønsted–Lowry base. (b) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate. (c) Describe a test for the ammonia produced.
items.answer: (a) Lone pair on N accepts a proton. (b) 21.2% (c) Damp red litmus paper turns blue.
items.markingKey: (a) Lone pair on N accepts a proton. [1] (b) 21.2% [2] (c) Damp red litmus paper turns blue. [1]

items.stem: A farmer in Auckland uses ammonium nitrate as a fertiliser. (a) Describe the shapes of NH₃ and NH₄⁺ and explain the difference in bond angle. (b) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate. (c) Describe a test for the ammonia produced.
items.answer: (a) NH₃ pyramidal 107° (one lone pair); NH₄⁺ tetrahedral 109.5° (no lone pair). (b) 35.0% (c) Damp red litmus paper turns blue.
items.markingKey: (a) NH₃ pyramidal 107° (one lone pair); NH₄⁺ tetrahedral 109.5° (no lone pair). [3] (b) 35.0% [2] (c) Damp red litmus paper turns blue. [1]

items.stem: What conditions are needed for photochemical smog to form?
options: sunlight acting on nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons
cold, dark conditions with no traffic
items.answer: sunlight acting on nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons
items.markingKey: Common in sunny, traffic-heavy cities.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how a catalytic converter reduces pollution from nitrogen oxides. (b) Explain why oxides of nitrogen form in car engines but not when the air is at room temperature.
items.answer: (a) NO is reduced to N₂ by reaction with CO (oxidised to CO₂) on the surface of a Pt/Rh catalyst: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. (b) The N≡N bond is very strong (high Ea); only at the very high temperatures in the engine do enough collisions have sufficient energy.
items.markingKey: (a) NO reduced to N₂, CO oxidised [1]; equation/catalyst [1] (b) strong triple bond/high Ea [1]; high temperature in engine [1]

items.stem: "A catalytic converter removes nitrogen oxides by oxidising them to nitrogen." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. NO is reduced to N₂ (oxidation number +2 → 0); CO is oxidised.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What type of catalyst is NO₂ in the atmospheric oxidation of SO₂? (b) What is the main source of sulfur dioxide in the atmosphere from human activity?
items.answer: (a) homogeneous (b) burning fossil fuels containing sulfur compounds
items.markingKey: (a) Gas-phase catalyst with gaseous reactants. (b) e.g. coal-fired power stations.

items.stem: Tomás investigates the effect of acid rain on limestone chips in a school laboratory. Explain how NO₂ acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of atmospheric SO₂.
items.answer: NO₂ oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ and is reduced to NO; NO is then oxidised back to NO₂ by oxygen, so NO₂ is regenerated.
items.markingKey: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂ regenerated [2]

items.stem: A coal-fired power station near Toronto releases sulfur dioxide. Explain how NO₂ acts as a catalyst for the oxidation of atmospheric SO₂.
items.answer: NO₂ oxidises SO₂ to SO₃ and is reduced to NO; NO is then oxidised back to NO₂ by oxygen, so NO₂ is regenerated.
items.markingKey: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; NO + ½O₂ → NO₂ regenerated [2]

items.stem: A power station in Nairobi burns 100 tonnes of coal containing 1.2% sulfur by mass. Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced.
items.answer: 2.40 tonnes

items.stem: Yusuf studies how SO₂ and NO₂ from a power station form acid rain. (a) Write an equation for the formation of sulfuric acid in rain. (b) Describe two effects of acid rain. (c) Suggest one way to reduce SO₂ emissions.
items.answer: (a) SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (b) Damage to buildings (limestone), death of fish in lakes, damage to forests, corrosion of metals. (c) Remove sulfur from fuels; flue-gas desulfurisation with CaCO₃/CaO.
